reason: The sources reliably corroborate more than a dozen distinct historical, observational, and physical claims about Jupiter's Great Red Spot across multiple independent sites.
story: Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a monster high-pressure storm towering five miles above surrounding clouds in the planet's southern hemisphere. Trapped without any solid planetary ground beneath it to slow its momentum, this counterclockwise vortex has raged for over three centuries. At its recorded peak, it spanned 25,000 miles wide—large enough to swallow Earth two to three times over. Over the last century, however, astronomers observed the giant shrinking by half. In 2019, telescopes caught the storm shedding massive flakes of red clouds, sparking alarm that the spot could vanish within decades. Yet fluid dynamicists explain that the visible clouds deceive us: the underlying vortex remains remarkably stable, fueled in part by swallowing smaller passing anticyclones. Even while shrinking, the solar system's greatest tempest easily dwarfs our entire world, churning with hurricane-shattering winds above 300 miles per hour.
angle: Even after shrinking for a century and shedding giant flakes into space, Jupiter's Great Red Spot is still an ancient, roofless monster storm large enough to swallow the entire Earth.

claims.claim: The Great Red Spot is an anticyclonic, high-pressure storm system.
The Great Red Spot is located in Jupiter's southern hemisphere.
The storm rotates in a counterclockwise direction.
The cloud tops of the Great Red Spot rise about 8 kilometers (5 miles) above surrounding Jovian clouds.
The storm has been observed and raging for at least 300 to 350 years.
Jupiter has no solid planetary surface, meaning there is no land friction to dissipate or weaken the storm.
Jupiter's atmosphere is composed primarily of hydrogen and helium.
Historically, the Great Red Spot was wide enough to contain two to three Earths.
Over the past century, the Great Red Spot has been observed steadily shrinking in diameter.
NASA's Voyager spacecraft flew past Jupiter in 1979 and returned detailed images of the Great Red Spot.
In spring 2019, astronomers observed the Great Red Spot shedding large flakes and blades of red clouds.
The Great Red Spot maintains its size and stability partly by absorbing smaller neighboring anticyclones.
The Great Red Spot's swirling clouds are cooler than neighboring clouds on Jupiter.
A smaller Jovian storm named Oval BA or Red Spot Junior formed from the merger of three white ovals.
In July 2006, the Great Red Spot and Red Spot Junior passed close to each other without colliding or merging.
A leading hypothesis suggests solar ultraviolet radiation alters atmospheric chemicals to create the storm's reddish color.

disputed: Whether 17th-century sightings by Cassini or Hooke represent the modern Great Red Spot or an earlier, extinct storm that dissipated before the 1831 spot formed; handle by attributing 17th-century observations to early telescope records and noting modern continuous tracking began in the 1800s.

Whether the shrinking cloud coverage and 2019 flaking signal that the storm is dying within decades, or if the underlying vortex remains intact; handle by presenting the debate between flaking observations and fluid dynamics models.
